title: A felled tree: does mobilising reserves change what you see?
question: After the crown comes off, does either of these look like a tree fighting back rather than just surviving? If they look the same to you, say so — that is the answer I need.
context_md:
Same tree, same seed, same cut: a band taken out of the crown at frame 12,000, roots untouched. Four stills at 1,400-frame intervals — the cut, then three stages of what grows back.

Today a cut tree is **less** able to rebuild than an uncut one: the budget for new shoots comes from intercepted light, so losing foliage lowers it. Measured over three seeds, a cut plant starts fewer shoots than an uncut one in every window after the cut — 7 against 59 on the worst. One arm here adds the opposite pull: a plant that has lost crown may spend reserves it is already holding on new shoots, in proportion to how much it lost.

**What I already know, so you do not have to look for it:** the shoot count moves a lot (65 → 108 after the cut, +66%) and the standing tissue barely moves (5,095 → 5,141, under 1%). So the question is whether 66% more shoots is worth anything *to look at*. I cannot tell, and that is the whole reason for this card.

Ignore the falling leaves and the rain — both arms have them.
